# File-type filtering in ripgrep

File-type filtering is what makes `rg -trust foo` search only Rust files. It lives
entirely in the `ignore` crate, in `crates/ignore/src/types.rs` and
`crates/ignore/src/default_types.rs`, and is wired into the CLI from
`crates/core/flags/hiargs.rs`.

## How definitions are represented

The shipped types are a flat table in `default_types.rs`:

```rust
pub(crate) const DEFAULT_TYPES: &[(&[&str], &[&str])] = &[
    (&["bat", "batch"], &["*.bat"]),
    (&["c"], &["*.[chH]", "*.[chH].in", "*.cats"]),
    ...
];
```

Each row is `(names, globs)`. The first element is a *list* of names, so a single
glob set can be registered under several aliases (`cs`/`csharp`, `py`/`python`).
`TypesBuilder::add_defaults` iterates the table and calls `add(name, glob)` for
every name × glob pair — aliases are duplicated definitions, not shared
references, so there are currently 202 rows but more names than that.

At runtime a definition is just a name plus its globs:

```rust
pub struct FileTypeDef { name: String, globs: Vec<String> }
```

`TypesBuilder` holds a `HashMap<String, FileTypeDef>` of definitions and a
separate, *ordered* `Vec<Selection<()>>` of what the user asked for
(`Selection::Select(name)` or `Selection::Negate(name)`). Keeping selections in a
vec rather than a set is what gives last-flag-wins precedence, described below.

`add` rejects the reserved name `all` and any name containing a non-alphanumeric
character (`Error::InvalidDefinition`). `add_def` parses the two user-facing
string forms: `name:glob` and `name:include:a,b,c`. The `include` form is
expanded eagerly at parse time — it copies the globs out of the referenced
definitions — so it can only reference types already defined, and later changes
to `cpp` will not propagate into a `src:include:cpp` defined earlier. `add_def`
validates that *all* referenced names exist before adding anything, so a partly
valid include leaves the builder untouched (asserted by `test_invalid_defs`).

Note that `select("all")` and `negate("all")` also expand eagerly, over whatever
is defined at that moment. `--type-add` after `-tall` is therefore not selected.

## Building the matcher

`TypesBuilder::build` walks the selections in order and, for each one, resolves
the name against the definition map (missing name → `Error::UnrecognizedFileType`,
which is how `--type-clear rust -trust` fails). Every glob of every selected
definition is pushed into one shared `GlobSetBuilder`, compiled with
`literal_separator(true)`, and a parallel `glob_to_selection: Vec<(usize, usize)>`
records which selection (and which glob within it) each set index came from. The
result is a single `GlobSet` covering selects and negations alike — the
select/negate distinction is recovered after matching, not encoded in the set.

`Types` also caches `has_selected` (true if any selection is a select) and an
`Arc<Pool<Vec<usize>>>` of scratch buffers for match results, so matching
allocates nothing per call and is safe to share across the parallel walker's
threads. `Types` is `Clone`; `hiargs.rs` clones it into the `WalkBuilder`, and
`dir.rs` wraps it in an `Arc`.

## Matching

`Types::matched(path, is_dir)`:

1. Returns `Match::None` immediately for directories or an empty glob set. Types
   never prune directories — a `-trust` walk still descends everywhere.
2. Extracts the **base name** via `pathutil::file_name` and matches only that.
   Type globs are basename globs; a glob containing `/` will never match.
3. Calls `set.matches_into(name, &mut matches)`, which yields matching indices in
   ascending order. The **last** index wins, since set indices follow selection
   order — so the last `-t`/`-T` flag on the command line decides.
4. If the winning selection is a negation → `Match::Ignore`, else
   `Match::Whitelist`, each carrying a `Glob` that exposes the responsible
   `FileTypeDef`.
5. If nothing matched: `Match::Ignore(Glob::unmatched())` when `has_selected`
   (whitelist mode — anything unrecognized is excluded), otherwise `Match::None`.
   The same fallback applies when `file_name` returns `None` (paths ending in `.`
   or `..`).

`Ignore::matched` in `dir.rs` consults types *after* `--glob` overrides and after
ignore-file rules, and only when `!types.is_empty()` (i.e. there is at least one
selection). That ordering is the source of the documented precedence: `-g` and
`.gitignore` both outrank `-t`.

## What a contributor should know

- **Adding a default type**: append a row to `DEFAULT_TYPES`, keep the list
  sorted lexicographically by the *first* alias (enforced by the
  `default_types_are_sorted` unit test) and wrapped to 79 columns. Glob syntax is
  globset's, including character classes such as `*.[chH]`.
- **Matching is case-sensitive**: `case_insensitive` is never set here, which is
  why `asm` lists both `*.s` and `*.S`.
- **Order is semantics.** Anything that reorders `TypesBuilder::selections`, or
  the order globs enter the `GlobSetBuilder`, silently changes precedence.
  `glob_to_selection` must stay index-aligned with the set.
- **`Error::InvalidDefinition` carries no detail**; if you extend `add_def`
  parsing, expect to improve the error type too.
- Tests live in `types.rs` (`matched!` macro over a synthetic type table) and end
  to end in `tests/misc.rs` (`file_type_add`, `file_type_add_compose`,
  `file_type_clear`, `type_list`). `--type-list` prints `Types::definitions()`,
  which is sorted by name with globs sorted within each definition, from
  `crates/core/main.rs`.
